title: Seneca close
hookLine: ninety days with a flawed, wise friend

cards: Close to ninety days ago, this path opened a letter that begins with a command: claim yourself for yourself.

Since then you've read a man who got seasick, wept too much, owned too much, flattered an emperor, tutored another, consoled grieving mothers, and died slowly with his friends around him. A flawed, wise friend.
Today the circle closes where it began, on the first page, and it reads differently now.

teach.b: Letter one opens: claim yourself for yourself, and gather up the time that's been taken from you, stolen, or let slip. Then the line that becomes today's carry: "Hold every hour in your grasp."
Back then it could sound like productivity advice. Now you know who wrote it: a busy man at the edge of a dangerous court, who had lost years to exile and would lose his life to an emperor's order.

Second, three ways time leaves. Some is snatched away, Seneca says, some is quietly taken, and some just slips. The most shameful loss comes from carelessness: not the hours stolen, but the hours let go without noticing.
Third, his honesty, already on page one. Seneca doesn't claim to waste nothing. He can't say that, he admits, but he can say what he loses, and why, and how.
He keeps the account. That's the whole friend in miniature: not perfect, but paying attention.
Fourth, the bottom of the jar. He ends with an old saying: thrift comes too late at the bottom of the jar, because what's left down there is the least, and the worst.
Start saving now, while the jar is still full. Seneca never pretended to be the sage. He was the friend in the next seat, working on the same lesson, and leaving it in writing.
Tomorrow, before Marcus Aurelius, he'll stand beside one more teacher.

how: Some readers of Seneca return to his first letter on time, and some keep a simple record of where their hours go, as he describes doing.

o: Seneca's habit of drinking only plain water from a jug
start saving your hours early, while there's plenty left
a store of coins kept safe for old age and hard times

p: what he loses, why and how

s: in Letter 1 Seneca claims he wastes no time at all
he says he can't claim that, but he can say what he loses, why and how.
Seneca says the worst loss of time comes from carelessness
worse than time snatched or stolen.
the 'bottom of the jar' saying means save what's left at the end
it means thrift at the bottom comes too late: start while the jar is full.

games.q: Lucilius writes back: and you, Seneca, do you waste no time? what does Letter 1 say?
o: I can't say that, but I can tell you what I lose, and why, and how.
games.why: he admits losses, and keeps the account. that honesty is there on the very first page.

practice: If you can, reread Letter one, which is short; if not, sit with what you remember of it. Then look back over yesterday and find one hour that went somewhere you didn't choose.
Don't scold yourself; just keep the account, the way Seneca did: what, and why, and how.

wordCard.voice: The jar, Seneca's closing image: thrift comes too late at the bottom of it, so start saving your hours now, while it's still full. Today's word.
